title: Fakes, not mocks

story: A backend function imports a scan: it uploads the file to object storage (S3 in production, MinIO on laptops and in CI) and then counts the files in the workgroup's folder. Its test replaces the storage client with a mock, a stand-in that accepts any call and returns whatever the test told it to. Last week someone changed the upload to a new bucket called scans. The test stayed green. In production every import failed with NoSuchBucket, because nobody had created that bucket.

The fix was one word: use the datasets bucket that every environment already has. And now the test is red, although the code finally works. The mock was wrong in both directions: green while production was broken, red as soon as the code was right.
hook.question: How do you replace a real service in tests with something that behaves like the real one, and how do you know it still does next month?

read.h: A mock records calls; a fake does the work
p: Here is the test from the story. MagicMock, from Python's unittest.mock, is the same idea as vi.fn(): an object that accepts any method call, returns what you configured, and remembers how it was called. The test then checks the call itself, assert_called_once_with("scans", ...). So the test proves that the code called put with these arguments. It proves nothing about whether real storage would accept the call, which is how the missing bucket got past the test. And because it checks how the code works instead of what it achieves, it breaks when the code changes in a harmless way.

A fake is a different kind of stand-in: a small, real implementation of the service that keeps its state in memory. A fake object store keeps the files in a dictionary, refuses to write into a bucket that does not exist, and returns the keys it really holds. The code under test cannot tell the difference, and the test can check outcomes instead of calls: after two imports, the workgroup has two files.

code.text:
from unittest.mock import MagicMock

from imports import import_scan


def test_import_scan_with_a_mock():
    store = MagicMock()
    store.list_keys.return_value = ["wg-1/a.csv"]
    assert import_scan(store, "wg-1", "a.csv", b"x") == 1
    store.put.assert_called_once_with("scans", "wg-1/a.csv", b"x")

notes.text: MagicMock accepts any method with any arguments, so a missing bucket can never fail here.
The test decides what storage "contains". Real storage is never asked.
This checks how the code works, not what it achieves, so a correct refactor turns it red.

read.h: Write the fake behind the same interface
p: A fake starts from the interface that the production code already uses, here a small ObjectStore class with create_bucket, put, get and list_keys. Python marks such an interface with ABC (abstract base class) and @abstractmethod, which is close to a TypeScript interface that a class must implement: a subclass that forgets a method cannot be created. The real adapter, S3Store, implements the methods with boto3, the AWS library for Python, and the fake, InMemoryStore, implements them with a dictionary of dictionaries.

Two habits make a fake worth having. First, be loud about errors, the way the real service is: a missing bucket raises NoSuchBucket in both implementations, because that is what S3 does, and a fake that quietly creates the bucket would hide exactly the bug from the story. Second, keep it small. A fake only needs the behaviour the code under test relies on, and it says in its docstring which tests prove it.

notes.text: Inherits the interface, so it must implement every abstract method.
The whole "storage": bucket name to (key to bytes).
Goes through _bucket, so writing into a missing bucket fails as it does on S3.
Sorted, because S3 returns keys in sorted order and the code may rely on it.
The same error type the real adapter raises, so callers handle one exception, not two.

read.h: The contract suite keeps the fake honest
p: A fake has the same weakness as a mock in the long run: the real service can change, or the fake can be "simplified" by someone in a hurry, and nothing notices. The answer is a contract suite: one set of tests that describes how the service behaves, run against the fake and against the real thing. In pytest that is a parametrized fixture. It yields the fake for one run of each test and a real MinIO for the second run, so every test runs twice.

The real side runs only when a real service is available. In the lab that means the MINIO_URL variable is set; in CI it is a job that already starts MinIO next to the tests. When the real service does something the fake does not, you add a contract test, watch it fail on the fake, and fix the fake. Then every test that uses the fake inherits the fix. A contract suite also catches bugs in the real adapter: S3 returns at most 1,000 keys per list call, and a contract test with 1,100 keys shows at once which side forgot to ask for the next page.

notes.text: The fake always runs. The real MinIO joins only when MINIO_URL is set, so the suite works on any laptop.
params makes pytest run every test that uses this fixture once per target, with ids [memory] and [minio].
A fresh bucket per test, so tests never see each other's keys on the shared MinIO.
The behaviour the story needed: a missing bucket is an error on both sides.

read.h: Put the fake in at the seam
p: In the lab, import_scan receives the store as a parameter, so a test can simply pass the fake. Real code often builds its own client instead, deep inside a service class. Then you look for the seam: the one place where production code creates or reaches the real service. You replace it there, and only there, with monkeypatch from the pytest lesson, so the rest of the code runs exactly as in production.

Remember the monkeypatch trap: replace the name in the module that uses it. If imports.py calls get_store(), you patch imports.get_store, and the fixture writes down in a comment why that is the seam. A fixture like this one is how every test that needs storage gets the fake, with no mock in sight.

notes.text: The seam: the only place that builds the real client.
Set up what every environment has, so the fake starts in a realistic state.
Replace get_store in the module that calls it. monkeypatch undoes this when the test ends.

deeper.h: Go deeper: fakes for a remote call and a job queue
p: The same idea works for services that are harder to imagine in memory. For a gRPC service (a remote-call protocol where a .proto file defines the methods and generated code sends them), the fake can be a real gRPC server inside the test process whose methods return in-memory answers, so the real client, the real encoding and a real socket are all tested. When it receives a method it does not implement, it answers with an error that names the method, so a gap fails a test instead of passing silently.

For a background job queue such as Celery, the fake records each job when the code sends it, after passing the arguments through the same serializer the real queue uses, and runs nothing until the test calls drain(). Then the test decides when the work happens, and an argument the real queue could not carry fails in the test, not in production.

lab.title: A fake object store with a contract suite
lab.goal: Watch a mock pass a broken import and fail a correct one, then write an in-memory fake whose contract suite runs against both the fake and a real MinIO.

guess.q: import_scan now uploads to a scans bucket that no environment has. The mock test and a test that uses the in-memory fake both run. What happens?

options.text: Both fail, because the bucket does not exist.
options.why: The mock has no idea what buckets exist. It accepts any call.

options.text: The mock test passes and the fake test fails with NoSuchBucket, just like production.
options.why: The fake keeps real state and is loud about a missing bucket, so it fails where S3 fails. The mock only checks that put was called.

options.text: Both pass, because neither talks to real storage.
options.why: Not talking to real storage is fine. Behaving like it is what matters, and only the fake does.

follow.say: Write the interface and the fake.
Write the real adapter, which turns S3's error into the same NoSuchBucket.
Write the code from the story, with its bug, and two tests: one with a mock and one with the fake.
follow.do:
cat > imports.py <<'EOF'
from store.base import ObjectStore


def import_scan(store: ObjectStore, workgroup: str, name: str, data: bytes) -> int:
    store.put("scans", f"{workgroup}/{name}", data)
    return len(store.list_keys("scans", prefix=f"{workgroup}/"))
EOF
cat > tests/test_imports.py <<'EOF'
from unittest.mock import MagicMock

import pytest

from imports import import_scan
from store.memory import InMemoryStore


def test_import_scan_with_a_mock():
    store = MagicMock()
    store.list_keys.return_value = ["wg-1/a.csv"]
    assert import_scan(store, "wg-1", "a.csv", b"x") == 1
    store.put.assert_called_once_with("scans", "wg-1/a.csv", b"x")


@pytest.fixture
def store():
    store = InMemoryStore()
    store.create_bucket("datasets")  # the only bucket every environment has
    return store


def test_import_scan_with_a_fake(store):
    assert import_scan(store, "wg-1", "a.csv", b"x") == 1
    assert import_scan(store, "wg-1", "b.csv", b"x") == 2
EOF

follow.say: Write the contract suite and run it on the fake only, as it runs on a laptop without MinIO.
follow.do:
cat > tests/test_store_contract.py <<'EOF'
import os
import uuid

import pytest

from store.base import NoSuchBucket
from store.memory import InMemoryStore
from store.s3 import S3Store

TARGETS = ["memory"] + (["minio"] if os.environ.get("MINIO_URL") else [])


@pytest.fixture(params=TARGETS)
def store(request):
    if request.param == "memory":
        store = InMemoryStore()
    else:
        store = S3Store(os.environ["MINIO_URL"], "minioadmin", "minioadmin")
    bucket = f"contract-{uuid.uuid4().hex[:12]}"
    store.create_bucket(bucket)
    return store, bucket


def test_put_then_get_returns_the_same_bytes(store):
    store, bucket = store
    store.put(bucket, "wg-1/scan.csv", b"id,age\n1,42\n")
    assert store.get(bucket, "wg-1/scan.csv") == b"id,age\n1,42\n"


def test_list_keys_filters_by_prefix_and_sorts(store):
    store, bucket = store
    for key in ["wg-2/b.csv", "wg-1/b.csv", "wg-1/a.csv"]:
        store.put(bucket, key, b"x")
    assert store.list_keys(bucket, prefix="wg-1/") == ["wg-1/a.csv", "wg-1/b.csv"]


def test_put_overwrites(store):
    store, bucket = store
    store.put(bucket, "k", b"old")
    store.put(bucket, "k", b"new")
    assert store.get(bucket, "k") == b"new"


def test_put_into_a_missing_bucket_raises(store):
    store, _ = store
    with pytest.raises(NoSuchBucket):
        store.put("no-such-bucket", "k", b"x")
EOF
uv run pytest -q tests/test_store_contract.py

follow.say: Now point it at the real MinIO too. Every test runs twice, once per target.

lab.build: Add delete(bucket, key) to the interface, to S3Store (boto3's delete_object) and to InMemoryStore. Write two contract tests: deleting a key removes it from list_keys, and deleting a key that never existed is not an error. Run the suite with MINIO_URL set. One test will fail on [memory] only: discover what real S3 does that your fake did not, and change the fake until all tests pass on both targets. Delete the mock test from tests/test_imports.py, since the fake test now covers it.
checks: Before the fix, the mock test passed and the fake test failed with NoSuchBucket: scans.
After switching to datasets, the mock test failed with expected call not found, and the fake test passed.
Without MINIO_URL the contract suite runs 4 tests; with it, 8, each marked [memory] or [minio].
Your delete tests pass on both targets, including a delete of a key that never existed.
When you are done, docker rm -f lab-minio removes the container.

solution.file: delete on both stores and its contract tests
solution.text:
# store/base.py: add to ObjectStore
    @abstractmethod
    def delete(self, bucket: str, key: str) -> None: ...

# store/s3.py: add to S3Store
    def delete(self, bucket: str, key: str) -> None:
        self._call(self.s3.delete_object, Bucket=bucket, Key=key)

# store/memory.py: add to InMemoryStore
    def delete(self, bucket: str, key: str) -> None:
        self._bucket(bucket).pop(key, None)  # S3 answers 204 for a key that never existed

# tests/test_store_contract.py
def test_delete_removes_the_key(store):
    store, bucket = store
    store.put(bucket, "wg-1/scan.csv", b"x")
    store.delete(bucket, "wg-1/scan.csv")
    assert store.list_keys(bucket) == []


def test_deleting_a_missing_key_is_not_an_error(store):
    store, bucket = store
    store.delete(bucket, "never-existed")

lab.fix: Someone made the fake "friendlier": in store/memory.py, put now runs self.buckets.setdefault(bucket, {})[key] = data, so writing into a missing bucket creates it. Make that change, change imports.py back to the scans bucket, and run uv run pytest -q. The fake test from the story passes again, so the fake now hides the production bug. Which test still catches it, and on which target? Undo the change so the fake is loud again.
explain: Why did the mock test pass when production failed, and fail when the code was fixed?
What does the contract suite prove that the fake's own tests could not?
The minio side runs only when MINIO_URL is set. Why is that acceptable, and where must it run so the fake stays honest?
lab.done: The contract suite, including your delete tests, passes 12 tests with MINIO_URL set, the fake is loud about missing buckets again, and lab-minio is removed.

check.q: A test patches the storage client with a MagicMock and asserts put was called with ("scans", key, data). What does a green run prove?

options.text: That the code called put with those arguments, and nothing about whether real storage would accept them.
options.why: A mock accepts every call. It cannot know the bucket is missing, so production can fail while the test passes.

options.text: That the file was stored and can be read back.
options.why: Nothing was stored anywhere. The mock only recorded the call.

options.text: That the scans bucket exists, because the mock would raise otherwise.
options.why: A MagicMock never raises unless you tell it to. It knows nothing about buckets.

check.q: Your contract suite has 10 tests, and they all pass on [memory]. MinIO is never started in any CI job. What is the weakness?

options.text: Nothing; passing on the fake is the goal.
options.why: Passing on the fake only proves the fake agrees with itself. The suite exists to compare it with the real service.

options.text: The suite is too small; it needs at least 50 tests.
options.why: Size is not the issue. A small suite run on both sides is worth more than a big one run on one side.

options.text: The real side never runs, so nobody would notice when the fake and the real service drift apart.
options.why: A contract only keeps the fake honest if the same tests also run against the real thing somewhere, for example in a CI job that already starts MinIO.

check.q: On the real MinIO, deleting a key that never existed succeeds. Your fake raises KeyError, and a new contract test shows it. What do you change?

options.text: Mark the test to run only on [minio], because the fake is stricter and that is safer.
options.why: A fake that is stricter than the real service fails tests that would work in production. It must behave like the real thing, not like your guess.

options.text: The fake, so it also accepts deleting a missing key (for example with dict.pop(key, None)).
options.why: The real service is the reference. Fix the fake, and every test that uses it gets the real behaviour.

options.text: The real adapter, so it also raises when the key is missing.
options.why: That would make S3Store disagree with S3 itself, and production code would get errors S3 never sends.

p: fcp's cloud talks to three things a unit test cannot run: the on-prem clients over gRPC, object storage (S3, or MinIO in CI) and Celery workers. Today the unit tests mock them in many places: 69 mock.patch calls on the gRPC client and 11 uses of CELERY_TASK_ALWAYS_EAGER, which runs a job inside the caller and skips the queue's serialization. The plan replaces those mocks in the new API test layer with three fakes, each pinned by a contract suite marked contract.

The object-store fake is this lab in fcp's own interface: it replaces AWSStorageServiceProvider at the seam where StorageService creates it, and its contract suite runs against the MinIO service that the cloud CI job already starts. The gRPC fake and the queue fake follow the ideas in the Go deeper panel.

tickets.why: InMemoryStorageProvider and its contract suite against MinIO: this lab in fcp's interface.
FakeOnPremClient: a real gRPC server in the test process that is loud about methods it does not implement.
FakeTaskQueue: records jobs through Celery's own serializer and runs them on drain(), checked against a real worker.
The rule for the new layer: no mock.patch of the gRPC client or storage, and no CELERY_TASK_ALWAYS_EAGER.

words.plain: A stand-in that accepts any call, returns what the test configured and records how it was called.
A small, working implementation of a service that keeps its state in memory and behaves like the real one.
One set of tests run against both the fake and the real service, so the two cannot drift apart unnoticed.
The one place where production code creates or reaches a real service, and where a test swaps in the fake.
Python's way to declare an interface: a class whose @abstractmethod methods every subclass must implement.

review.q: In one sentence each: what does a mock test prove, and what does a fake test prove?
review.a: A mock test proves the code made certain calls. A fake test proves the code reaches the right outcome against something that behaves like the real service.

review.q: Sketch the fixture that runs a contract suite on a fake and, when available, on the real service.
review.a: @pytest.fixture(params=["memory"] + (["minio"] if os.environ.get("MINIO_URL") else [])), build the fake or the real adapter from request.param, give each test a fresh bucket, and return it.

review.q: The real service starts returning a new error for a case your fake accepts. What are your three steps?
review.a: Write a contract test for that case, watch it fail on the fake (and pass on the real side), then change the fake until both sides pass.

remember: Test outcomes against a fake that keeps real state, and run one contract suite on the fake and the real service so the fake stays honest.
